usamts-2007-r3-01.title: Geometric series
usamts-2007-r3-01.body:
Count the cubes by generation.
* Generation $0$: one cube of volume $1$.
* Generation $1$: one cube on each of the $6$ faces, side $\frac13$, volume $\frac1{27}$ each.
* Each new cube is attached by one face, so it has $5$ exposed faces, each of which receives a cube one-third as large. Hence generation $n \ge 1$ has $6\cdot 5^{n-1}$ cubes, each of volume $\left(\frac1{27}\right)^n$.

(The cubes do not overlap: everything growing out of the $+x$ face of the unit cube stays within $|y|, |z| \le \frac16 + \frac19 + \frac1{27} + \dots = \frac16 + \frac16 = \frac13 < \frac12$, so the six branches are disjoint from each other and from the unit cube; the same argument works at every scale.)

Total volume:
$$1 + \sum_{n=1}^\infty 6\cdot 5^{n-1}\cdot\frac1{27^n} = 1 + \frac{6}{27}\sum_{m=0}^\infty\left(\frac{5}{27}\right)^m = 1 + \frac{6/27}{1 - 5/27} = 1 + \frac{6}{22} = \frac{14}{11}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{14}{11}$**

usamts-2007-r3-01.title: Self-similarity
usamts-2007-r3-01.body:
Let $V$ be the volume of one "branch": a cube of side $1$ attached by one face, together with everything that grows on its other $5$ faces. Each of those 5 faces carries a copy of the branch scaled by $\frac13$, whose volume is $\frac{V}{27}$. So
$$V = 1 + 5\cdot\frac{V}{27} \implies V = \frac{27}{22}.$$
The whole sculpture is the unit cube plus $6$ branches scaled by $\frac13$:
$$1 + 6\cdot\frac{1}{27}\cdot\frac{27}{22} = 1 + \frac{3}{11} = \frac{14}{11}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{14}{11}$**

usamts-2007-r3-02.title: Stars and bars
usamts-2007-r3-02.body:
Let $a, b, c, d$ be the numbers of times Gene chooses the top-left, top-right, bottom-left and bottom-right $2\times2$ squares. The final grid depends only on these counts (not on the order):
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|}\hline a & a+b & b\\\hline a+c & a+b+c+d & b+d\\\hline c & c+d & d\\\hline\end{array}$$
Different quadruples give different grids, since the corners are $a, b, c, d$.

All entries lie in $[1, 12]$ exactly when the corners are $\ge 1$ (then every entry is $\ge 1$) and the centre $a + b + c + d \le 12$ (the centre is the largest entry). So we count positive integers with $a + b + c + d \le 12$.

Put $e = 13 - a - b - c - d \ge 1$. Then $a + b + c + d + e = 13$ in positive integers: place 4 dividers in the 12 gaps between 13 objects in a row, giving
$$\binom{12}{4} = 495 .$$

**Answer: $495$**

usamts-2007-r3-02.title: Sum by the centre value
usamts-2007-r3-02.body:
With $a, b, c, d$ as in the first solution, the number of positive solutions of $a + b + c + d = k$ is $\binom{k-1}{3}$. Summing over the possible centre values $k = 4, \dots, 12$:
$$\binom33 + \binom43 + \dots + \binom{11}{3} = 1 + 4 + 10 + 20 + 35 + 56 + 84 + 120 + 165 = 495,$$
which is $\binom{12}{4}$ by the hockey-stick identity.

**Answer: $495$**

usamts-2007-r3-03.title: Congruences and CRT
usamts-2007-r3-03.body:
For a polynomial with integer coefficients, $f(x) = x\,g(x) + f(0)$ with $g$ having integer coefficients, so $f(n) \equiv f(0) \pmod n$ for every integer $n$. Hence
$$f(0) \equiv 2007 \pmod 7, \qquad f(0) \equiv 2007 \pmod{200}.$$
Since $\gcd(7, 200) = 1$, the Chinese Remainder Theorem gives $f(0) \equiv 2007 \equiv 607 \pmod{1400}$. The only number in $(0, 2007)$ congruent to $607$ modulo $1400$ is $607$ (the next ones are $-793$ and $2007$). So $f(0) = 607$ for every such polynomial.

Such polynomials exist, e.g. $f(x) = 2007 - (x - 7)(x - 200)$, which has $f(0) = 2007 - 1400 = 607$.

**Answer: $f(0) = 607$**

usamts-2007-r3-03.title: Factor out the roots
usamts-2007-r3-03.body:
The polynomial $f(x) - 2007$ has integer coefficients and roots $7$ and $200$. Dividing by the monic polynomial $(x-7)(x-200)$ keeps integer coefficients, so
$$f(x) = 2007 + (x-7)(x-200)\,g(x)$$
with $g$ having integer coefficients. Then $f(0) = 2007 + 1400\,g(0)$ with $g(0)$ an integer. The condition $0 < f(0) < 2007$ forces $-\frac{2007}{1400} < g(0) < 0$, i.e. $g(0) = -1$, so $f(0) = 607$.

**Answer: $f(0) = 607$**

usamts-2007-r3-04.title: Reduce the blocks modulo 101
usamts-2007-r3-04.body:
Let $N_n$ be the number consisting of $n$ copies of $2007$. Then
$$N_n = 2007\left(1 + 10^4 + 10^8 + \dots + 10^{4(n-1)}\right).$$
Since $10^2 = 100 \equiv -1 \pmod{101}$, we get $10^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{101}$, so every term $10^{4k} \equiv 1$ and
$$N_n \equiv 2007\,n \pmod{101}.$$
Now $2007 = 19\cdot 101 + 88$, so $N_n \equiv 88n \pmod{101}$. Since $101$ is prime and does not divide $88$, $101 \mid N_n$ exactly when $101 \mid n$. In particular $N_{101}, N_{202}, N_{303}, \dots$ are all divisible by $101$, which gives infinitely many. ∎

usamts-2007-r3-04.title: Pigeonhole
usamts-2007-r3-04.body:
Consider $N_1, N_2, \dots, N_{102}$. Two of them, say $N_i$ and $N_j$ with $i < j$, leave the same remainder modulo $101$, so $101 \mid N_j - N_i = N_{j-i}\cdot 10^{4i}$. Since $\gcd(101, 10) = 1$, $101 \mid N_{j-i}$. So some $N_k$ ($k \ge 1$) is divisible by $101$.

Then all $N_{k}, N_{2k}, N_{3k}, \dots$ are divisible by $101$, because $N_{mk} = N_k\left(1 + 10^{4k} + 10^{8k} + \dots + 10^{4k(m-1)}\right)$. Hence infinitely many members of the set are multiples of $101$. ∎

usamts-2007-r3-05.title: Distance of centres, then a double count
usamts-2007-r3-05.body:
**Setup.** Index the circles by pairs $(r, s)$ of integers with $s \ge 1$, $0 \le r \le s$ and $\gcd(r, s) = 1$: the circle has centre $\left(\frac rs, \frac{1}{2s^2}\right)$ and radius $\frac1{2s^2}$. The pairs $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$ give the two circles of diameter 1, and the other pairs give the circles for $0 < \frac pq < 1$. Distinct pairs give distinct fractions $\frac rs$.

**(a)** The radius of each circle equals the $y$-coordinate of its centre, so each circle lies in the upper half-plane and touches the $x$-axis at $\left(\frac rs, 0\right)$. Take two circles $(r_1, s_1) \ne (r_2, s_2)$. Since they touch the axis at different points, neither can lie inside the other or be internally tangent to it; so they meet in two points exactly when the distance $d$ between their centres is less than the sum of radii $\rho = \frac1{2s_1^2} + \frac1{2s_2^2}$. Compute
$$d^2 - \rho^2 = \left(\frac{r_1}{s_1} - \frac{r_2}{s_2}\right)^2 + \frac14\left(\frac1{s_1^2} - \frac1{s_2^2}\right)^2 - \frac14\left(\frac1{s_1^2} + \frac1{s_2^2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{r_1}{s_1} - \frac{r_2}{s_2}\right)^2 - \frac{1}{s_1^2s_2^2} = \frac{(r_1s_2 - r_2s_1)^2 - 1}{s_1^2 s_2^2}.$$
Since $\frac{r_1}{s_1} \ne \frac{r_2}{s_2}$, the integer $r_1s_2 - r_2s_1$ is nonzero, so its square is at least $1$ and $d^2 - \rho^2 \ge 0$, i.e. $d \ge \rho$. Hence the two circles are either disjoint or externally tangent: they share at most one point. (Tangency does occur, e.g. for $(0,1)$ and $(1,1)$.)

**(b)** The circle $(r, s)$ has area $\pi\left(\frac1{2s^2}\right)^2 = \frac{\pi}{4s^4}$, so we must show $\sum_{(r,s)} \frac{1}{s^4} = 1 + \frac{\zeta(3)}{\zeta(4)}$, where $\zeta(k) = \sum_{i\ge1} i^{-k}$.

Consider all pairs of integers $(a, b)$ with $0 \le a \le b$, $b \ge 1$, each weighted by $\frac1{b^4}$. All series below have positive terms and converge, so they may be rearranged freely.
* Summing over $b$ first: for each $b$ there are $b + 1$ choices of $a$, so the total is $\sum_{b\ge1}\frac{b+1}{b^4} = \zeta(3) + \zeta(4)$.
* Every such pair can be written uniquely as $(a, b) = (nr, ns)$ with $n = \gcd(a, b) \ge 1$ (note $\gcd(0, b) = b$) and $(r, s)$ one of our index pairs. So the total is also
$$\sum_{(r,s)}\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{n^4s^4} = \zeta(4)\sum_{(r,s)}\frac1{s^4}.$$

Equating, $\sum_{(r,s)} \frac1{s^4} = \frac{\zeta(3) + \zeta(4)}{\zeta(4)} = 1 + \frac{\zeta(3)}{\zeta(4)}$, and multiplying by $\frac\pi4$ gives the total area
$$\frac\pi4\left(1 + \frac{\sum_{i\ge1} 1/i^3}{\sum_{i\ge1} 1/i^4}\right).$$
(By (a) the circles do not overlap, so this is also the area of their union.) ∎
